title: $\text{DT}^\text{2}$: Decision-Targeted Digital Twins
claim: Models with lower step-wise error can still rank decisions incorrectly, while a less accurate model can preserve the correct ordering.
layout: 2 stacked panels, left-to-right time axes, shared legend, green target band
description: Two stacked line-plot panels share one legend at the top. The legend has a green band for optimal glucose, faded solid lines for true rollouts, and bold dashed lines for DT rollouts. Both panels start from a black history curve that ends at a black dot. Three treatment trajectories fan out from that dot in blue (high), purple (adaptive) and orange (low). Each panel has a horizontal green band for the optimal glucose region on a grey background. The top panel, Φ̂1, has dashed rollouts that sit close to the true curves, but the purple one drifts out of the green band. The bottom panel, Φ̂2, has dashed rollouts that sit farther from the true curves, but the purple one stays inside the band while blue and orange leave it. The eye goes first to the green bands and the dashed curves.
caption: We visualise two diabetes DTs, ˆΦ1 (top) and ˆΦ2 (bottom), under treatment plans with high, low, and adaptive insulin levels, and we consider the ‘value’ of a treatment plan as the time it spends in the optimal glucose region. ˆΦ1 has lower MSE from the true rollouts, yet it leads to an incorrect treatment plan preference ordering (high ≈low ≻adaptive). In contrast, ˆΦ2 leads to a correct preference ordering (adaptive ≻high ≈low), despite its higher MSE, as its rollouts traverse the correct glucose regions.
abstract: A digital twin (DT) is a virtual model of a real-world system that can assist decision-making by simulating scenarios induced by different policies. However, typical machine learning-based DTs do not optimise for this use case. We prove that, when model capacity is limited, training DTs to minimise one-step transition errors can produce suboptimal models for ranking sets of policies according to a reward function. We further show that this holds empirically, even with expressive model classes. To address this, we introduce $\text{DT}^2$, a decision-targeted DT training paradigm. Firstly, $\text{DT}^2$ uses fitted Q-evaluation to estimate values of candidate policies from offline data. A DT is then trained to generate rollouts that preserve pairwise policy rankings derived from these proxy ground-truth values with an architecture-agnostic loss function. We empirically demonstrate the efficacy of our method across a range of settings and architectures. $\text{DT}^2$ consistently improves policy ranking and reduces decision regret during policy selection relative to conventional DT training, both for policies used during training and for unseen policies, while maintaining a good level of raw simulation fidelity.
